title: The heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:17–40)
hookLine: Moses, Rahab, Gideon, and unnamed ones of whom the world was not worthy
tomorrow: what do you say to someone whose knees have given up?
last: THE EVIDENCE OF THINGS NOT SEEN.

cards: At the end of a movie, the credits roll past the stars and keep going: the driver, the caterer, the person who held the light. Most people are already walking out. Hebrews eleven has credits like that.

Halfway down its list, the writer runs short of time: "And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets."
The names come faster and faster. And then they stop, and a plainer word takes over: others.

teach.b: The named ones first. Moses "refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter." Rahab of Jericho "received the spies with peace."
Some on this list won. They "stopped the mouths of lions," and "out of weakness were made strong."
But others didn't win. They were mocked, chained, driven out, and "wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins." No names at all.

teach.h: OF WHOM THE WORLD WAS NOT WORTHY.
teach.b: And right there, mid-sentence, the writer stops to add: "Of whom the world was not worthy." The world counted them as nobody. Hebrews turns it around: the world wasn't good enough for them.
Then a twist: "And these all, having obtained a good report through faith, received not the promise." Not even the well-known ones.
God, the writer says, had something better in view, "that they without us should not be made perfect."
So what does this give you for an ordinary week? A new way to read the room.
The person refilling the coffee, the aide on the night shift, the neighbor who always shows up: Hebrews puts people like that in the same chapter as Moses, and gives them its highest line.

how: Christians remember the faithful of Hebrews 11 in sermons and study, and some churches also keep days to remember saints and believers whose names are not known.

games.q: what does “the heroes of faith” mean?
o: the kings who won Israel's greatest wars
the faithful of Hebrews 11, named and nameless
the saints whose names fill church windows

games.q: who's in the credits — tap the pairs.
p: refused to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son
of whom the world was not worthy

s: everyone in Hebrews 11's list won their battle
some did; others were mocked, chained and driven out, and wandered in sheepskins.
Hebrews 11 names every faithful person it describes
the names stop, and the writer says others, of whom the world was not worthy.
even the well-known names received not the promise
that they without us should not be made perfect.

games.q: at your great-aunt's funeral, the program thanks the pastor, the soloist, the pallbearers. nobody mentions the neighbor who drove her to every appointment. what does Hebrews 11 do with people like that?
o: leaves them out; lists are for the well-known.
says they'll get their names in a later list.
gives them its highest line: the world was not worthy.
games.why: Hebrews runs out of names and keeps going: others, of whom the world was not worthy. the unnamed get the chapter's most honoring words.

practice: Count three people whose work you leaned on today without knowing their names: who stocked the shelf, drove the bus, cleaned the hallway, answered the phone.
Give each one a slow breath and a silent thank you, the way Hebrews gives the unnamed a line of their own.

wordCard.voice: The heroes of faith. The crowded end of Hebrews eleven: Moses and Rahab, and the others whose names nobody kept.

orig.note: Greek: worthy. Hebrews 11:38, of whom the world was not worthy.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the world was not worthy, said of people with no names in the story. Peace to you.
